title: Harvard Tells International Students to Return Before September 15 Visa Overhaul
excerpt: New DHS rule replaces open-ended student visa stays with four-year caps and shifts extension filings from universities to federal immigration services.
body:
• Harvard is urging international students on F-1 and J-1 visas to be in the U.S. before September 15, when new DHS rules replace the "duration of status" system with fixed admission periods.
  • Students already in the country when the rule takes effect will retain current protections, including 60-day grace periods; those who re-enter after September 15 face stricter terms.
  • The rule caps student visa stays at four years and shifts extension responsibility from universities to USCIS, adding cost and bureaucratic burden.
  • A coalition of education groups and unions has filed a federal lawsuit to block the rule, but no injunction has been granted.

Harvard University is advising its international students and scholars to return to the United States before September 15, when a sweeping new Department of Homeland Security rule will fundamentally alter how F-1 and J-1 visa holders maintain their immigration status.

The Harvard International Office issued the guidance last week, warning that the rule — published on July 17 and set to take effect in three weeks — will apply differently to students depending on whether they are in the country when it goes into effect.

The September 15 Dividing Line

Under the current system, international students on F-1 visas can remain in the United States for the "duration of status" — essentially as long as they maintain valid enrollment in their academic program. The new rule replaces that open-ended framework with a fixed admission period, capped at four years.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2091807357206749251

Students already present in the U.S. on September 15 will be authorized to stay until the later of their program end date or the expiration of eligible post-completion work authorization, up to a maximum of four years. They will also retain the existing 60-day grace period for F-1 holders and 30-day period for J-1 holders.

But students who leave the country and re-enter after September 15 will become subject to the new rules upon reentry. Their I-94 admission records will carry a fixed "Admit Until Date" tied to the program end date, and the F-1 grace period will be shortened to 30 days.

Extension Burden Shifts to Students

Perhaps the most significant practical change involves how students extend their stays. Under the existing system, universities can generally update a student's program dates without a separate federal application. The new rule requires students to file directly with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for extensions, a process that involves biometric vetting, background checks, and fraud screening, according to DHS.

The rule also restricts students' ability to transfer between institutions or change their programs of study — changes that could complicate academic planning for graduate students pursuing longer research programs.

"We understand that the rule change, and the lack of clarity surrounding it, has been confusing and unsettling for all of us across higher education."

— Harvard International Office guidance

Legal Challenge Pending

A coalition of higher education organizations and labor unions, including the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, filed a lawsuit on August 18 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts seeking to block the rule. The plaintiffs have asked for a preliminary injunction, arguing the changes are "arbitrary and capricious" and that DHS failed to adequately justify them despite more than 20,000 public comments — many of them critical.

"They will discourage foreign students and other nonimmigrants from coming to the United States, repelled by the intolerable prospect of losing lawful immigration status partway through their studies," the lawsuit states. A DHS spokesperson dismissed the suit as "performative."

No injunction has been granted, meaning the September 15 deadline remains the working assumption for universities and students.

Impact on Indian Students

Indian students constitute one of the largest groups of international students in the United States, with tens of thousands holding F-1 visas at any given time. Many pursue graduate programs in STEM fields that extend well beyond four years, making the fixed-term cap particularly consequential.

Harvard President Alan Garber warned in July that the four-year limit is "odd" for doctoral programs and could deter international students from pursuing Ph.D.s in the United States. He estimated that international student enrollment has already fallen roughly 20 percent nationwide, with effects most visible among postdoctoral scholars.

Students from India considering travel home during the fall semester should review their visa documents, Form I-20 or DS-2019, and I-94 records, and consult their university's international office before booking flights.

What's Next

With no injunction in place, September 15 remains the effective date. Universities across the country are issuing similar guidance to their international communities. The lawsuit could still result in a court order blocking the rule, but timing is uncertain. Harvard noted in its guidance that "the outcome of litigation is uncertain" and pledged to communicate any changes.
